body:
RossG12345 <rossg12345@aol.com> wrote:
: Scrapie,
: 	Hi Peter!
: 	You say  "I believe that the death and injury counts in both 
: of those cases are greater than Kaczynski's."  Isn't this irrelevant?

No.  If people really care about death and injury then numbers matter.
If you say killing is bad then that includes killing several hundred
thousand Iraqis to protect the U.S. interest in low gasoline prices
and the other examples discussed.  You can't pick or choose between
which examples of death adn injury are significant.  It's all numbers.

: In the Pinto case, it was a cost-benefit analysis.  The auto
: executives estimated the value of a human life to be $100,000, 
: and accordingly, found the design acceptable in light of the
: projected number of fatalities.  Understandably, the jury 
: found the calculation unacceptable.  And was outraged even
: that any such calculation would be done.  Ralph Nader fought for
: years to draw attention to the problem and did so without killing.

You're confusing the facts like a good lawyer.

Nader was fighting a single issue of human deceit and harm, while Dr.
Kaczynski was fighting dozen and dozens of issues.  The Pinto case is
just an example while Dr. Kaczynski was fighting the core issues.  If
Dr. Kaczynski had approached things like Nader then he would have be
able to complete only one or two things by now and the main problem
would still persist.

Incidents like the Pinto case still occur, except now companies are 
smarter and don't document their perverse logic that justifies imposing
harm to customers.  Also undocumented are the methods of designing
items that have an intentionally short lifespam built in so that
people will have to come back and buy again.  We're not as stupid at
building things as the commercial world makes things seem.  It's just
not profitable to build something that lasts.  Disposible items makes
money change hands and so it is "good for the econonmy" though the serfs
suffer.

: In the case of the tobacco companies and the lobbyists and lawyers
: who work for them, they calculate that 300,000 a year will die
: from the marketing of the product, but rationalize that what they
: do is legal, very profitable and a matter of a smoker's free choice.  
: All the companies have known to make a safe cigarette -- eliminating
: nicotine, tar and carbon monixide --  but it wouldn't sell (at least
: not as well) because it would taste terribly, not burn as well, not
: be addictive etc.

Sure, creating an addiction is no harm and if it's ok in the eyes of the
law then it's somehow moral.  Good legal-speak!

Sometimes things that are legal are still harmful to people and in the
cases of the legal drugs tobacco and alcohol, far more people die from
those than the illegal ones.

: And, so it goes, there are moral calculations involved in each.

And legal solutions to moral problems aren't the best way of dealing
with things.

: But with respect to serial murder and blowing up planes, though,
: if an auto safety zealot or anti-smoking zealot started killing
: people and detonating bombs on airplanes in order to draw 
: attention to their views, the fact that these other executives 
: and professionals have made immoral shameful
: decisions in no way excuses the immoral act or a murderer who
: set out to kill innocents as a publicity stunt.

Agreed, but only because those small problems can actually be pursued
and people made accountable.  But you can't make anyone accountable for
the things that Dr. Kaczynski was pointing out.  There is no possibility
for negotiations or even of admittance of wrongdoing, so the only solution
remaining for someone who cares is to try to take matters into their own
hands.  Thats the profound existential paradox here: a man with a PhD
seeking all possible alternatives and then reluctantly finding that the 
only solution is for him to send bombs to the enslavers of mankind and
to urge others to revolt against technology.  He knew how crazy that was
but it was also the most honest solution and the only one that would fix
the underlying problem.  Now how do you communicate that to someone who
is addicted to technology and won't listen to a thesis suggesting that
reliance on technology and ostricization of nature are harmful behaviors?

: Kaczynski has 
: brought discredit to the anti-technology views -- and by urging destruction of
: everything, he makes those people who argue against certain technologies (e.g.,
: cloning of humans) that much more 
: difficult.

Rather he illuminates the problem by anticipating it.  When the cloning guy
says that science can't be stopped, the rest of us should have recognized the
madman Dr. Kaczynski spoke about in his essay that would push science on
the rest of us.

180.  The technophiles are taking us all on an utterly reckless ride into
the unknown.  Many people understand something of what technological
progress if doing to us yet take a passive attitude toward it because they
think it is inevitable.  But we (FC) don't think it is inevitable.  We
think it can be stopped, and we will give here some indications of how to
go about stopping it.

: The role of David's brother is very good reason not to apply
: the death penalty, and the prosecution has virtually no chance 
: (less than 5 % ) of getting a death sentence.  But Kaczynski's 
: intellectual justifications simply don't count for much -- 
: otherwise animal rightists, anti-abortionists, and on and on 
: would also be able to justify the murder of innocents.

This is more important than a single issue.  Dr. Kaczynski is fighting
dozens of issue that are of great significants, not merely a matter of
political taste.  The future of humanity is on the line.

: At the same time we take a stand against blind acceptance of
: advances in science -- Richard Seed's (the wannabe clone-guy)
: view that "We can't stop science -- we need to take the moral 
: stand against murder.  It's not inconsistent to admire the manifesto
: and embrace his anti-technology ideas and at the same time 
: despise him.  Otherwise, we've failed the families who have lost 
: their loved ones.

The families are not important because they were led by sick men who
were trying to harm humanity with their greedy and selfish "progress".

H.W.
